questions.q: Which two modalities require near-absolute-zero or high-vacuum operating conditions, according to the comparison in this lesson?
options: Superconducting and photonic
Photonic and neutral-atom
Trapped-ion and neutral-atom
Superconducting and trapped-ion
questions.explain: Superconducting qubits need a dilution refrigerator near absolute zero, and trapped-ion systems need high vacuum and laser cooling, while photonic and neutral-atom systems both operate at or near room temperature.

questions.q: What is identified as the biggest open scaling bottleneck specifically for photonic quantum computing?
options: An inability to route photons through any kind of waveguide
The need for a dilution refrigerator to reach millikelvin temperatures
Photon loss during routing and detection, which has no direct error-correction analog
A complete lack of any native connectivity between qubits
questions.explain: Photon loss is singled out as photonic computing's central bottleneck because a lost photon, unlike a decohering stationary qubit, cannot be recovered or directly corrected.

questions.q: What is identified as a real open engineering challenge for neutral-atom platforms, alongside their genuine advantage of large raw atom counts?
options: Gate fidelity, atom loss during trapping/excitation, and connectivity risk during array rearrangement
Requiring a larger dilution refrigerator than any other platform
An inability to operate at room temperature
A complete absence of reconfigurable connectivity
questions.explain: Neutral-atom systems genuinely scale well in raw atom count, but gate fidelity gaps, atom loss, and the risk of losing atoms during 2D/3D rearrangement remain real, unresolved engineering challenges.

questions.q: Why does the lesson conclude that there is 'no universal winner yet' among the four modalities?
options: Because all four modalities are functionally identical and the comparison doesn't matter
Because superconducting qubits have already been proven superior on every metric and the other three are obsolete
Because quantum computing hardware comparisons are purely a matter of opinion with no factual basis
Because each modality leads on some axes (such as speed, fidelity, temperature, or connectivity) while having a real, unresolved weakness on others -- none dominates across every axis that matters
questions.explain: The comparison shows each modality has genuine strengths (e.g., ion fidelity, superconducting speed, photonic room-temperature operation, neutral-atom raw scale) paired with a real, named weakness -- which is exactly why no single one dominates every axis today.

questions.q: According to the lesson's closing guidance, what should you ask whenever a quantum hardware company announces a record (most qubits, highest fidelity, fastest gate)?
options: What's being measured, under what conditions, and what isn't being claimed alongside it
Whether the record was set using a superconducting platform, since only those claims are worth scrutinizing
Only whether the company is well-funded, since funding level determines the claim's accuracy
Nothing -- any announced record should be accepted at face value regardless of modality
questions.explain: The lesson's core transferable skill is scrutinizing any record claim -- a big qubit count without a fidelity number, or a high fidelity number without array-wide context, tells you less than it first appears to, regardless of which modality is making the claim.
